doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Clarinet duets with Hugh Young and the hand-made fake book
summary: Playing duets with Hugh Young, early recordings, and his hand-copied fake book of melodies that helped him as an arranger.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: He played along already when he was 12 or 13 years old. I couldn’t do that. He had a good ear. Maybe not perfect pitch. But then I knew chords and I started to get better as an improviser, as I listened to the greatest — that’s the thing, I listened to the greatest players. So the melodic thing. So when I’m playing with his he’s playing a melody and I’m playing one note out of the chord. I didn’t know ninths yet and elevenths and sharp

thirteenths whatever. (There’s no sharp thirteenth, sharp eleventh). But I would play a note [scats]. And then we’d improvise a little bit and we recorded, when recorders first came out, these big heavy recorders. Like “My Fair Lady,” my parents had that, we recorded that. So we, and the other thing two with me, my dad was an artist as a hobby. Cartoonish caricature kind of things. So I was pretty good in art, better than most kids. And I made a fake book, a B flat fake book for tenor and clarinet, which I read out of. The two of us would read this. And it was, all the melodies were in black ink with the real ink, not Pentel or anything. And the titles and chords are in colored pencils with ruler I’d use, so it was very neat. So I had about a hundred tunes. I was very meticulous, disciplined, crazy that way. But my point with melody is, because I learned all these melodies from the fake book and we played these and I heard all the melodies, even waltzes that might have been a little corny, I mean if you wrote the tune you’d be a millionaire, but all the old tunes, and then I had one of the first play-a-longs with the guitar strum [scats] and I’m play the clarinet and I’d swing, uh squeak I mean. But I was so happy at 13 years old to be able to play a melody like these professionals. So if you could play a couple of licks that you copied, I don’t even remember. So that was the thing why I think I was really good as one of, as a pick, to happen to be one of the arrangers with Blood, Sweat & Tears as with Dick Halligan.
